title: Equality of opportunity in supervised learning
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NIPS 2016), Barcelona, Spain, 5-10 December 2016; eds D. Lee, M. Sugiyama, U. Luxburg, I. Guyon and R. Garnett; Curran Associates, Inc.
harvard_reference: Hardt, M., Price, E. and Srebro, N. (2016) 'Equality of opportunity in supervised learning', in Lee, D., Sugiyama, M., Luxburg, U., Guyon, I. and Garnett, R. (eds) Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NIPS 2016). Barcelona, Spain, 5-10 December. Curran Associates, Inc., pp. 3315-3323. Available at: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2016/hash/6a9659feb1216f14f7384ba499518b38-Abstract.html (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
abstract_summary: The paper proposes an 'oblivious' non-discrimination criterion for supervised learning, equalized odds, which requires the predictor Y-hat to be independent of the protected attribute A conditional on the true outcome Y; in the binary case this means equal true-positive rates and equal false-positive rates across groups. It introduces a weaker relaxation, equal opportunity, which imposes the constraint only within the advantaged outcome Y=1 (i.e. equal true-positive rates). The authors show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor or real-valued score to satisfy either criterion by a post-processing step that uses group-specific (for equalized odds, possibly randomized) thresholds chosen by a small linear program on the group-conditional ROC curves, minimising the loss in utility. They prove that applying this post-processing to a Bayes-optimal regressor yields the Bayes-optimal non-discriminating classifier, quantify the cost when the score is sub-optimal, discuss the inherent limits of oblivious measures for identifying discrimination, and illustrate the framework with a case study of FICO credit scores.

claims_supported.claim: Equalised odds requires equal true-positive and false-positive rates across groups; equal opportunity relaxes this to the true-positive rate; both can be achieved by post-processing thresholds.
claims_supported.where: Section 2, Definition 2.1 and the sentence following the binary-case formula: 'For the outcome y = 1, the constraint requires that Y-hat has equal true positive rates across the two demographics A = 0 and A = 1. For y = 0, the constraint equalizes false positive rates.' Section 2.1, Definition 2.2: equal opportunity requires Pr{Y-hat=1 | A=0, Y=1} = Pr{Y-hat=1 | A=1, Y=1}, introduced as 'a relaxation of equalized odds ... only within the advantaged outcome group' and described as 'a weaker, though still interesting, notion of non-discrimination'. Post-processing: Introduction (contributions): 'Rather than changing a possibly complex training pipeline, the result follows via a simple post-processing step that minimizes the loss in utility.' Section 2.2 (end): 'equalized odds predictors can be derived from [scores] and the protected attribute A, by using different (possibly randomized) thresholds depending on the value of A. The same is possible for equality of opportunity without the need for randomized thresholds.' Section 4 ('Achieving equalized odds and equality of opportunity'), Definition 4.1 (derived predictor), Proposition 4.4 (linear program) and the paragraphs 'Deriving an optimal equalized odds threshold predictor' / 'Deriving an optimal equal opportunity threshold predictor' (Figure 2). Abstract: 'we show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor so as to remove discrimination according to our definition.'

caveats: The paper's equal-opportunity definition is stated relative to the 'advantaged' outcome Y=1 (e.g. not defaulting on a loan), so in a churn setting the report should say which class is coded as Y=1 and that equal opportunity equalises the true-positive rate for that class only. For equalized odds the optimal post-processed predictor may require randomized (mixed) thresholds per group, whereas equal opportunity can be met with deterministic per-group thresholds; the report should not imply both are always plain deterministic threshold shifts. The optimality results (Corollary 5.3, Theorem 5.6) assume the post-processing starts from a (near) Bayes-optimal score, and the method requires access to the protected attribute at decision time.
